newsitem.title: USA: Argentina dollar debts shine in peso bond's wake.
newsitem.headline: Argentina dollar debts shine in peso bond's wake.

text.p: Argentina's Brady bond prices were buoyed by spillover demand from the peso bonds which rallied after Wednesday's successful placement of the 500 million peso-denominated 10-year Eurobond, traders said.

The bond, offered in the U.S. under section 144-A of the Securities and Exchange Commission regulation to qualified institutional investors, was twice oversubscribed and many retail investors scrambled to buy pro-1 and pro-2 peso bonds, which have similar maturity in 2007, traders said.
The new peso bond was bid above par, just shy of 101, according to a Eurobond trader, noting, "The high yield is attracting lots of European buyers."
The buying spree pushed Argentine dollar-denominated FRBs and PARs higher, squeezing spreads 10 and 15 basis points tigher respectively, Brady traders said.
Argentina FRBs ARFLC05=RR rose 1/2 point to 89-1/2 and Argentina Pars AR4C23=RR 5/8 to 64-5/8.
Elsewhere, the positive tone in the U.S. Treasuries brought the sidelined buyers back into emerging markets.

Brazil Bradies belatedly reacted to the market-friendly development on late Tuesday when the Lower House passed the constitutional amendment to allow President Henrique Cardoso to run for a second term, traders said.
Brazil C BR8D14=RR climbed 5/8 to 76-3/4 and Brazil Pars BR4D24=RR added 1/2 to 63-7/8.
Even Ecuador papers shrugged off news that the government is wateering down austerity moves in the face of popular protest, casting a growing shadow on the ambitious economic reform proposal.
Among the measures announced by Finance Minister Pablo Concha annouced late Wednesday were the suspension of price increases for utilities and raising some part of the minimum wage.
Ecuador Pars ECPARS=RR rose 1/2 to 71.00 and Ecuador PDI ECPDI=RR gained 1/4 to 64-7/8.
The slide in Bulgaria's bond prices halted before the U.S. trading began Thursday morning, and short-covering became the order of the day, traders said.

"The trend is not good," said a trader with a U.S. investment house, noting that the continued plunge of its currency indicated the confidence was thin and the possibility of defaulting on the country's foreign debt remained high.
